"The intelligence ombudspersons consider that there are currently no newly emerged significant factual circumstances that would provide grounds for initiating an investigation," Justas Gaidys, senior adviser at the office, said in a comment to BNS. Gaudys said the decision not to investigate was based primarily on the fact that the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) had already carried out an inquiry into the alleged prison more than a decade ago on the instruction of the Seimas. He also noted that the Prosecutor General's Office is continuing a reopened pre-trial investigation and that the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has already delivered three judgments concerning the detention of individuals at alleged CIA facilities in Lithuania. "Recognising that this issue remains significant to the public, the Ombudsperson plans to initiate an inter-agency dialogue with the competent Lithuanian authorities," Gaidys said. "The aim of this dialogue will be to assess the possibilities of obtaining new information, determine whether any additional action falls within the ombudspersons' remit, and build a comprehensive understanding of the situation," he added. Debate over the alleged CIA prison resurfaced after Lithuania lost its third case before the ECHR in July. The Strasbourg court awarded 30,000 euros to Saudi Arabian national Abd Al Rahim Hussein Al-Nashiri over his unlawful detention at a secret CIA prison in Lithuania. The court also ordered the Lithuanian authorities to seek assurances from Washington that the terrorism suspect would not face the death penalty. Allegations that the CIA operated a secret detention facility in Lithuania first emerged in 2009, when US broadcaster ABC News reported that eight terrorism suspects had been held near Vilnius between 2004 and 2005. Later that year, the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) concluded that it could not establish whether detainees had been transferred to Lithuania, but found that the conditions for such transfers had existed. Earlier this year, the Prosecutor General's Office confirmed that it is continuing its investigation into the alleged unlawful transportation of people across Lithuania's state border. Any further probe should be handled by an inter-agency commission, she added. "An inter-agency commission should investigate, if we were to form one. [...] We need to decide who actually has the competence to investigate and present arguments in a way that leaves no doubt in the future," TamaÅ¡unienÄ told reporters on Wednesday. https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-new.text: Poland is on India's side when it comes to fighting terrorism because "we are victim" of it, Polish envoy Piotr Antoni Switalski has said, asserting that his country supports India's "right to pursue terrorists everywhere they go".In his response to a query during a press interaction after an event on Thursday, Switalski, however, did not elaborate on his comments.Earlier in his address at an event hosted by the Centre for Integrated and Holistic Studies, the envoy said that Poland sees India as a very "effective partner", and the two countries can do things together, especially when the world has become a very unpredictable place, and there are "many disruptive forces"."We can build really an axis of stability, predictability, and good model for the global governance" and send a "good signal" to the outside world by doing good things together, he added. India-Poland cultural tiesThe Polish ambassador to India also underlined the cultural ties between the two countries, and mentioned the benevolent roles played by the then Maharaja Jam Sahib of Nawanagar, Sir Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, who had sheltered Polish children during the World War II.He is known in Poland as the "Good Maharaja" and there is a Good Maharaja Square in Warsaw."He is a very emotional factor which makes for India, a special place in our hearts, the hearts of Poles," the envoy said. Switalski also spoke of a museum coming up in Kolhapur to mark the benevolent act of the then royal family of Kolhapur, which was at the forefront of giving shelter to Polish women and children displaced due to the horrors of World War II.Between 1942 and 1948, around 5,000 Polish refugees found shelter in Valivade, near Kolhapur, after being displaced by the tragedy of the Second World War.The settlement grew into a vibrant 'Little Poland', complete with schools, a church, and community life, offering hope and dignity to families far from their homeland, the Polish embassy had said in a social media post in June.In 2019, a memorial pillar was unveiled and the foundation for a museum was laid to preserve the memory of the Polish refugees who lived in Valivade.The museum is now nearing completion and ready to serve as a place where members of the Polish diaspora can reconnect with their family histories and the remarkable legacy of India's humanitarian spirit, it said.Poland sees India as defence partnerThe envoy said Poland is spending billions of euros on procurement, "and, we see India as a very attractive partner" because in some areas of defence production, India is very advanced and it has the scale.‘We support your right to pursue terrorists’Later, interacting with reporters, he said, "on the question of terrorism, we are on your (India's) side, because we are victim of terrorists"."You cannot compare, because the terrorist acts committed on Indian soil in the past years, including in Kashmir in 2025, were terrible. Nothing comparable happened in Poland. But we are on your side, and our voice, we said openly, we support your right to pursue terrorists everywhere they go. Because our policy on that is very clear. And we said it openly," the envoy said.On reports that Polish drones were used against Pakistani infrastructure in the first days and hours of Operation Sindoor, he said, there were reports by Indian sources, but also Pakistani sources."They shot down some of them, some of the drones, Polish drones," he said, adding that he suspected that they were "simply used as decoys, and they were training drones, and this is what experts were telling."The envoy said when he hears any statement using the Pakistani factor to attack Poland, "I'm really very surprised. And I suspect sometimes, a kind of foreign agenda behind it."Poland eyes wider economic cooperationIn his address, he also said Poland sees India as a "very effective partner" and is ready to work with it in agriculture and other fields, and "our companies are ready to work with you.""Some of the Indian companies are investing and operating in Poland. And I'm very glad, because Poland should be considered by your companies, as a friendly gateway to the European Union, to its big market, half a billion consumers," he said.He underlined that Poland and India may have a great asymmetry in terms of their sizes, and separated by thousands of miles, with rivers, seas, oceans, mountains, deserts, separating them."But, as we know, geography is a superficial measure of distance. As they say, true closeness is measured by the mind, the spirit, and the tongue. And I want to take you on a journey that reveals that Poland and India are not distant strangers, but ancient structural cousins, bound by a profound historical and emotional architecture," the envoy said.He underscored how the Polish language uses words which have roots in Sanskrit, and added that even his surname has Sanskrit roots."When Poland and India are looking at each other, we are looking into a mirror," he said."We can do things together, in times when the world has become a very unpredictable place, where the situation is quite turbulent, where you have so many disruptive forces. When you look at India and Europe, and Poland in particular, you can see that we can build really an axis of stability, predictability, and a good model for global governance," the envoy said."And that's probably why our relationship… When I say Poland, I mean also the European Union, is much more important than simply bilateral dimension. We can send a good signal to the outside world, by doing good things together," he said.

Photograph: Ana Escobar/EPA Weather tracker Spain Analysis Weather tracker: Thunderstorms hit Spain as Japan braces for typhoon James Michelin for MetDesk At least one person dead as stormy weather causes severe flooding in Barcelona and Valencia Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.36 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 06.22 EDT Share Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person . Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region. Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia . With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely. In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period. Tropical Storm Dujuan, currently over the open west Pacific Ocean, will move north-west on a track towards Japan over the coming days. It is forecast to intensify into a category one typhoon on Friday. The joint typhoon warning centre is forecasting that Dujuan will skirt past the south-east coast of Japan, potentially affecting Tokyo and the surrounding areas. https://www.politico.eu/article/vladimir.text: President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party secured a majority in the State Duma, Russia’s lower house, following the country’s first parliamentary elections since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. In a widely expected result, the ruling party won around 58% of the vote for the 225 deputies elected via party lists, according to preliminary data from Russia’s Central Election Committee. Another 225 will be elected in single-mandate seats, where United Russia candidates are also dominating. Voting took place over the course of three days, with polls closing Sunday evening. The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the elections “marked another major setback for Russian democracy” and their outcome “was never in doubt.” Advertisement Advertisement “I have proposed measures against those facilitating these sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territories,” she added. Residents of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — regions that the Kremlin unlawfully occupied after the 2022 assault started — also took part in the vote, with some reportedly coerced into doing so . The war in Ukraine featured heavily in the elections , which were marked by severe repression. Dissenting voices were all but silenced, and Yabloko — the country’s only openly anti-war party — was banned from fielding a national list of candidates in the State Duma. “A party that has not been represented in the country’s parliament for 23 years [would have] secured second place in the polls, given the conditions in which we operate,” said Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov following the elections . “And the authorities could do nothing about it other than remove the party from the election.” Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said of the results : “The citizens of our country maintain their trust in our leading political force [Putin’s party] and consider it appropriate to continue entrusting it with governance at various levels of state authority.”

Posted on 10/29/2026 3:14:10 PM PDT by UMCRevMom@aol.com WASHINGTON -- Former US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo says Russian President Vladimir Putin has shown no willingness to end his war against Ukraine, warning that Moscow’s growing cooperation with Beijing, Tehran, and Pyongyang poses a serious challenge to Western security. In an interview with RFE/RL on October 29, Pompeo, who served in President Donald Trump’s first administration, discussed Ukraine’s prospects for peace, the risks of negotiating with Putin, Iran’s support for Moscow, and the need for stronger Western security guarantees for Kyiv. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. RFE/RL: With a fresh round of attacks on the ground, mounting pressure on Kyiv, and high-stakes diplomatic maneuvering, the situation appears to be shifting quickly in Ukraine. What are you observing on the ground, and how do you assess the current calculus? Mike Pompeo: What I think everyone is seeing is that we are not yet at a point where Vladimir Putin has demonstrated any willingness to back off on his terror campaign, and that's precisely what he's been engaged in. The costs clearly, in his judgment, don't exceed the benefits of him continuing this conflict. And so you're right; he's trying to make this an incredibly difficult winter for the Ukrainian people, not for the Ukrainian military. The Ukrainian military is crushing him, -- 42,000 casualties a month -- but [he's targeting] the Ukrainian people...to convince the political leadership -- and frankly, the political leadership in Washington and in Brussels and in European capitals -- that it's not worth continuing the support that they've provided to Ukraine to date. RFE/RL: Can Washington and its allies afford to trust any diplomatic framework offered by Vladimir Putin right now? I think Putin is wrong in his judgment that he is winning." Pompeo: Well, the answer to that is no, but that doesn't mean you don't continue to pursue diplomacy, right? But you don't believe a single thing that he says. You simply observe the actions that he takes. But it's not unheard of to talk to someone that you don't trust. In the end, you try to develop a framework and agreement, and then you sign it, and then you watch it be executed, and you believe it only when the execution takes place. And so, you know, the fact that he's been unwilling to even conduct more than just the most minuscule cease-fires. Right now, there's this temporary, short-term ceasefire in one town (Oleshky, in Russian-occupied southern Ukraine). When [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy has agreed to broad cease-fires on energy, on agriculture at the Black Sea, has agreed to [and] publicly announced that he'd be prepared to take a cease-fire along the military lines as they currently exist, that is radically different from the obstinacy with which Vladimir Putin has treated the discussions. RFE/RL: President Zelenskyy warns that Ukraine is facing severe, compounding political and military pressure. Is the West inadvertently pushing Kyiv into bad-faith concessions? Pompeo: I can't imagine that Kyiv will ultimately take a bad concession. They've been at this too long. They've been fighting too hard. They've frankly been too successful, with, by the way, enormous support from the United States and Europe. So, I suspect that President Putin's belief that he can convince the West to drive Kyiv to the table to take a bad deal will prove not to be an outcome that is ultimately achieved. I think Putin is wrong in his judgment that he is winning. RFE/RL: What does a realistic, secure end-state look like that doesn't simply plant the seeds for another Russian invasion? Pompeo: That's perhaps the most important question. What is the outcome that defends Western civilization adequately? I think the answer to that is less dependent on where the lines are. It tends to be that that's the focus of the] conversation. What's more important is that there is a long-term commitment, a security architecture that makes the cost of the next advance by Vladimir Putin simply unacceptable. That would be whether it's NATO or non-NATO. I don't know that that's as important, but European non-Ukrainian forces on the line would make an attack that happened after the agreement is implemented and in place truly an attack on the West, not simply an attack on Ukraine. RFE/RL: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov is set to visit Atlanta for the G20 ministerial this weekend. What is the single most important line in the sand the United States must draw for him face-to-face? Pompeo: Oh, goodness, it's a line that, frankly, Americans haven't been prepared to draw to date, right? Nor has Europe, right? I've seen the critiques, including mine, that the diesel agreement -- that President Trump recently said we take some Russian diesel -- I don't think it solves the energy problem for America, nor do I think it draws us any closer to a negotiated solution. But, frankly, the Europeans continue to spend enormous amounts of money upholding the Russian war machine, right? That's hypocrisy. "Critical" is the nicest thing one can say about that. And so it's not about what they say to Lavrov in Atlanta this weekend. It's about the actions that the West is prepared to take to support Ukraine's effort to defend its border from this terrorist attack, this aggressive terrorist attack that has so harmed European sovereignty. RFE/RL: President Zelenskyy has also raised concerns about restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink access affecting defensive drone operations. Given your multiple recent visits to Kyiv and the region, and your firsthand look at Ukrainian command centers, how dangerous is it when technology companies' decisions disrupt frontline military operations? Pompeo: You know, it's complicated. I mean, the easy answer is it's very dangerous. I've seen multiple explanations for what actually happened: who said what to whom, and when, and how long it actually was. Was the speed limited? I don't know. I don't know what to make of those, other than there seems to be a consensus that there was a limitation for a period of time. That's very difficult for the Ukrainian forces. Having said that, one of the hallmarks of Ukrainian success is that they have been able to deliver autonomous solutions by themselves, a set of capabilities that they have delivered, not dependent on anyone from any place else. I think this highlights for every nation the fact that they need their own set of capabilities to do what's necessary. I'm very happy that the United States continues to support Ukraine with intelligence assistance and with an American product developed by an amazing American company, right? Developed by Elon [Musk] and his team. But it does highlight the fact that we need to be good partners in that effort. RFE/RL: You've warned for years that Moscow isn't acting alone, and that we're witnessing a coordinated effort between Russia, Beijing, and Tehran to systematically undermine Western security. Are we witnessing a formal wartime alliance or simply a coalition of convenience aimed at neutralizing American power? Pompeo: You know, it's interesting. I don't know that it matters that much which of the two it is. It is clear that there is an alliance. It is clear that they are working together. It would really be Pyongyang, Beijing, Tehran, and Moscow working together. And it would have been the Venezuelans, but we've taken down that risk materially... They have many disagreements with each other. They'll find places where they can't cooperate. But on destroying Western civilization, this is something they all agree on. These are a collective set of leaders who don't give a rip about human life, who don't give a rip for basic property rights, who don't care remotely about religious freedom. They share that common set of understandings. Their principles and their values reflect that understanding of humanity. And so, when they can advance that vision for how the world ought to look, they will work together, even in spite of the fact that they'll have disagreements among themselves. You see it at the tactical level with weapons systems, with electronic components, with tactical and even strategic-level intelligence sharing. But more importantly, you see it at the senior-leader level, at the nation-state level, where these countries have clearly demonstrated their willingness to work together to undermine that post-World War II architecture that has been so good for the United States, so wonderful for Europe, and frankly amazing for freedom all around the world. RFE/RL: Given that cooperation, is the current Western defense strategy sufficiently equipped to deter a multitheater conflict involving China in the Indo-Pacific and Russia in Europe simultaneously? Does the West have the military capacity and strategy to handle both theaters at once? Pompeo: Look, I'll cut to the bottom line. We're going to crush them. That is, to prevail, but it's going to take an enormous amount of determination. It's going to take amazing political leadership. It's going to take European leaders who are prepared to talk to their people about why it is the case that they have this responsibility, why it's in Europeans' best interest. Every [EU] nation, all two dozen-plus of them, needs to work to deliver good outcomes for their own people. That means spending money, it means training soldiers, it means participating in your military and your strategic efforts. This will take real political leadership, and I hope people across the world can see what happens to nations that aren't prepared to do that. If you don't defend your borders, you end up with Islamists inside your country. If you don't secure your own freedom by developing a military capable of participating in this civilizational effort, then the bad guys will try to take advantage of it, and every nation has to do this to protect its own sovereignty and to work at it diligently. I'm convinced we will all do that, but there's a lot of work that remains. RFE/RL: What concrete steps should the United States and its allies take today to dismantle the supply lines connecting Tehran to Moscow? Pompeo: Yes, so there are many things. There are, I'll call them, tactical and military measures that one can take, right? You can stop ships from sailing. You can interdict goods. The United States has done that with the Europeans, and, frankly, others were more actively engaged in that. The economic pressure that the United States is putting on Iran and Tehran's leadership is very real. You know, [US Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent has talked about weeks [for a possible collapse of Iran's economy]. I don't know if it's just weeks, but it will happen. This regime will collapse. As we saw with the Soviet Union, you can't predict the day or the hour or even the year, but the regime cannot possibly withstand the combination of the blockade that sits in place, the economic pressures that have been applied, and, I hope, the continued effort, the continued kinetic efforts that President Trump has indicated he may well be prepared to undertake in the coming weeks as well. This will give the Iranian people the chance to do what's necessary. We will be able to tip the regime over in a way that delivers an outcome that is remarkable for the Iranian people, incredibly important for the Gulf Arab states and Israel, and enormously valuable to the United States of America as well. ARTICLE Ukraine war latest: ‘Russia’s mass murder’ — Deadly Russian strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk The Kyiv Independent news desk October 29, 2026 9:42 pm https://kyivindependent.com/ukraine-war-latest-russias-mass-murder-deadly-russian-strikes-on-dnipro-chernihiv-kremenchuk/ Key developments on Oct. 28: ‘Russia’s mass murder:’ Drone strike on Dnipro station kills 14 amid deadly daytime attacks on Chernihiv, Kremenchuk Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says Route demining completed in Russian-occupied Oleshky as humanitarian convoy prepares to enter, Ukraine’s ombudsman says Ukraine strikes Russian ‘drone port’ in Bryansk Oblast, damaging storage facilities, military says UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast Russian general charged in absentia for missile strike on museum dedicated to 18th century Ukrainian philosopher Russian forces struck a train platform at Dnipro railway station on the morning of Oct. 29, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 more, authorities said. A passenger train was preparing to depart the platform for Zaporizhzhia when the station was attacked by a Russian jet-powered drone, Ukrainian Railways wrote on social media. The brazen daytime attack was followed in close succession by deadly strikes against civilians in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk. The strikes on civilians come not only in the middle of a scheduled local ceasefire in Kherson Oblast, agreed to by Kyiv and Moscow to help evacuate and deliver aid to the residents of the occupied city of Oleshky, but also ahead of the first trilateral “peace negotiations” mediated by the United States since February this year. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Dnipro was attacked around 11:00 a.m. by four Russian jet-powered drones, three of which were downed by Ukrainian air defense before reaching their targets. Despite the air raid alert and announcements of a heightened threat, people remained on the platform, Ukrainian Railways said. Passengers were told to evacuate from the stationary train around ten minutes before the strike, with station and train staff checking each train car one by one. At 11:29 a.m., Dnipropetrovsk Oblast governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported that medics were already at the scene of the attack, providing first aid. “A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station,” President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack. “The Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing.” “How many such terrorist attacks has Russia carried out on our people after lifting sanctions on some Russian oligarchs and energy companies instead of de-escalating.” Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze described the attack on Dnipro as “mass murder.” Following the Russian attack on Dnipro, 25,000 people in the city and surrounding Oblast were left without electricity, Hanzha said in the afternoon. Later in the day, Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov reported that a Russian drone struck the dormitory of a vocational school in Dnipro, setting the entire fifth floor on fire. There were no injuries, Filatov said, as the students had managed to reach the shelter before the strike. Throughout the day, Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured four more people, including a 15-year-old girl, Hanzha said in an evening statement. Elsewhere across Ukraine, the cities of Chernihiv and Kremenchuk were also targeted by daytime Russian attacks. Around noon, Russian forces struck the center of Chernihiv in northern Ukraine with Banderol cruise missiles, killing two 15-year-old girls, regional governor Viac
